solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Quiet English officer in retro bar

indicators.note: retro means looking backwards, so the word is read from end to start
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a pub is a bar
E is the abbreviation for English
LT is short for lieutenant

explanation.surface: A quiet Englishman in uniform sits in an old-fashioned pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet' looks like an adjective for the Englishman, but it is the definition as a command; 'retro' only turns the bar round.
explanation.definitionFit: Belt up is a blunt British imperative telling someone to stop talking, just like the command Quiet!

clue.text: City no longer safe when leader is deposed

indicators.note: a deposed leader is removed from the top, so the first letter goes

blocks.note: ex means former, no longer so
peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: A city that was once secure has seen its ruler overthrown.
explanation.walkthrough: PETER is underworld slang for a safe (a peterman cracks them); dropping its P and adding EX gives EXETER.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeter is a cathedral city and county town of Devon in south-west England.

clue.text: Pamphleteer’s article about a month going round part of Europe

indicators.note: going round means turning about, so this pair is read backwards
about means surrounding, so the outer word wraps the rest

blocks.note: the definite article
taken as written
MO is short for month
Spain is a country in Europe

explanation.surface: A pamphlet writer's piece concerns a month spent touring part of Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'a month' is turned round; the article then wraps everything. The possessive stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Paine wrote the famous political pamphlet Common Sense, urging American independence in 1776.

clue.text: Tap part of body around start of this medical procedure

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter only
one thing placed around another encloses it

blocks.note: to pat is to tap lightly
the chest is part of the body
first letter of this

explanation.surface: A doctor taps a patient's chest to begin an examination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tap' sounds like the doctor's action, but it is just the first chunk of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A patch test applies a small amount of substance to the skin to check for an allergic reaction.

clue.text: Cancels fresh order of rolls right away in cheap eatery

indicators.note: a fresh order means a new arrangement of the letters
something sent away is taken out of the word
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
a caff is British slang for a cheap cafe

explanation.surface: Someone cancels a new order of bread rolls straight away at a greasy spoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right away' reads as immediately, but it means remove the R; a caff is British slang for a cheap cafe or greasy spoon.
explanation.definitionFit: To call off an event or plan is to cancel it, a common phrasal verb synonym.

clue.text: Officer leading lots of people across lake in small boat

indicators.note: leading means going in front, so this piece comes first
stretching across something means spanning it on both sides, enclosing it

blocks.note: CO is a commanding officer
a race is a large group of people
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: An officer leads a crowd across a lake in a tiny boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots of people' is a race in the sense of a people or nation, not a running contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A coracle is a small round Welsh boat of wicker covered with hide or tarred cloth.

clue.text: Somewhat uplifted future volleyball fan

indicators.note: somewhat means only a part, so the letters sit within the words
in a down clue lifting up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: Someone who will love volleyball feels a bit uplifted.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of 'future' and 'volleyball' and read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A lover of something is an enthusiast or devotee, which is what a fan is.

clue.text: Group siesta every other missed …

indicators.note: missing every other letter keeps only the alternate ones

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A group misses every other siesta and the thought trails off into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to 8 Down but plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A set is a collection of things or people belonging together, a standard synonym for group.

clue.text: … because nobody rises in the morning

indicators.note: in a down clue something that rises reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: for can mean because
no one means nobody

explanation.surface: Continuing from 7 Down: the siestas are missed because nobody gets up in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins the two surfaces; the wordplay is self-contained.
explanation.definitionFit: Forenoon is a dated word for the part of the day before noon, which is the morning.

clue.text: Writer of articles about wine — European reds, principally

indicators.note: principally means first and foremost, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
port is a fortified wine
E is the abbreviation for European
first letter of reds

explanation.surface: A wine writer pens articles mostly about European red wines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer of articles about wine' looks like one phrase, but 'about' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A reporter is a journalist who writes news stories and features for a newspaper or broadcaster.

clue.text: Devout sort not half bleary after five religious books

indicators.note: not half means losing half the word, here its first three letters

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral five
OT is the Old Testament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pious person grows bleary-eyed after reading five religious books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' removes the front half here, keeping the back three letters; the Old Testament counts as religious books.
explanation.definitionFit: A votary is someone bound by vows to religious life, or a devoted worshipper.

clue.text: Free wild animal man had brought round about

indicators.note: bringing something round another encircles it
about can mean turned about, facing the other way

blocks.note: he'd is the contraction of he had
a wildcat is a cat

explanation.surface: A man has brought a wild animal back and set it free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man had' is the contraction he'd; the container is built first and only then reversed as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: To free something is to unfasten or separate it, a verb synonym of detach.

clue.text: Verger finally collected money after church service

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so the last letter is kept
collected letters are gathered and composed anew
coming after means placed behind

blocks.note: CE is the Church of England
last letter of verger
taken as written

explanation.surface: A verger takes the collection plate round at the end of a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collected' reads as the verger gathering money, but it signals the rearrangement of R and MONEY.
explanation.definitionFit: A ceremony is a formal religious or public occasion, and a service is one kind held in church.

clue.text: Pantomime cat showing up thus in tights

indicators.note: in a down clue showing up means read from bottom to top
being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat
hose are tights or stockings
ergo is Latin for therefore, thus

explanation.surface: A pantomime cat appears on stage in tights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pantomime cat' looks like Puss in Boots, but pantomime alone is the definition; British pantomime is a comic family stage show at Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother Goose is a traditional British Christmas pantomime, the seasonal comic stage show for families.

clue.text: In courtyard, dislike new display

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: a patio is a paved courtyard
to resent is to dislike bitterly
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone in a courtyard dislikes a new exhibition.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma is punctuation only; the new letter goes on the end after the container is made.
explanation.definitionFit: A presentation is a showing or exhibition of something to an audience, which is a display.

clue.text: Familiar melody from opera company, French one

blocks.note: the Met is the Metropolitan Opera in New York
une is French for one

explanation.surface: A well-known tune comes from a French opera company.
explanation.walkthrough: The opera company is THE MET, the Metropolitan Opera; 'French one' is UNE, the feminine form.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme tune is the recognisable signature music of a programme or film, heard so often it becomes familiar.

clue.text: Repeatedly check gauge of railway for train

blocks.note: CH is the chess abbreviation for check
OO gauge is a standard model railway track size
the pair is said twice

explanation.surface: A railway inspector keeps checking the track gauge for a train.
explanation.walkthrough: CH and OO together, then the same again; OO is the popular gauge for model railways.
explanation.definitionFit: Choo-choo is a child's word for a railway engine, imitating the sound of a steam locomotive.

clue.text: Mostly the vicar seems distraught when his busy time begins?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a time, standing for the noun

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
someone distraught is all over the place, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: The vicar looks frantic as his busiest season is about to start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' applies only to 'the', which loses its E; the question mark flags the definition as a description of a date rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Clergy are at their busiest over Christmas, which starts with midnight mass on the evening before Christmas Day.

clue.text: Plug record on telly, regularly showing proficiency

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: an ad plugs a product
an EP is an extended-play record
third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Someone skilfully plugs their new record on television.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternate letters are taken from 'on telly' starting at the third; telly is British for television.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something adeptly means doing it with skill and expertise, so it shows proficiency.

clue.text: Seafood and beef, you say?

indicators.note: you say points to the spoken form rather than the spelling

blocks.note: beef means brawn or muscle

explanation.surface: A surf-and-turf dish of shellfish and beef.
explanation.walkthrough: Beef as a noun means physical strength or brawn, which is the spoken word here.
explanation.definitionFit: A mussel is an edible bivalve shellfish, one example of seafood.

clue.text: One hundred — too old for treatment

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
over age means too old

explanation.surface: A centenarian is judged too old for medical treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Treatment' suggests medicine, but it is the media sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Coverage is the way news media report and handle a subject, i.e. their treatment of it.

clue.text: Girl disconcerted rival

indicators.note: someone disconcerted is thrown into disorder, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl has unsettled her competitor.
explanation.walkthrough: Girl in crosswords usually signals a female first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Avril is a female given name, and crosswords routinely use girl for any woman's name.

clue.text: For instance, award winning item of pottery?

blocks.note: e.g. means for instance
GC is the George Cross, a British gallantry award
a side that is up is ahead, winning

explanation.surface: An award-winning piece of pottery is held up as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Award winning' looks like one adjective; it is two pieces. The George Cross is Britain's top civilian award for bravery.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg cup is a small ceramic holder for a boiled egg, and the question mark admits not all are pottery.

clue.text: Ship with loud speaker one disconnected

indicators.note: something disconnected is cut off and removed

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for with
a hailer calls out loudly, as in loud-hailer
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A ship carries a loudspeaker, one of which has been unplugged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loud speaker' is read as a person who hails, not an audio device.
explanation.definitionFit: A whaler is a vessel used for hunting whales, so it is a kind of ship.

clue.text: Smoker to think over giving up in the end

indicators.note: giving up the end means losing the final letter
turned over means flipped, reading the other way

blocks.note: to mull is to think carefully

explanation.surface: A smoker considers quitting eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoker' suggests a person, but it is the thing that smokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Lum is a Scots and northern English word for a chimney, something that gives out smoke.

clue.text: City‘s to disappoint fans, are we told?

indicators.note: being told means hearing it, so the spoken sound counts

blocks.note: a team losing disappoints its fans

explanation.surface: A city's team is set to let down its supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is an idea rather than a synonym: what disappoints fans is their team losing.
explanation.definitionFit: Toulouse is a major city in south-west France, famous for its rugby team.

clue.text: Classmate? Precisely

blocks.note: the whole word is the wordplay, split into its two parts in the blocks that follow
a form is a school class
an ally is a friend or mate

explanation.walkthrough: 'Classmate' looks like one word but splits into two; form is the British school term for a class.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something formally means in a correct, exact and ceremonious way, so precisely.

clue.text: Cleric visits cathedral city regularly

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside the place being visited

blocks.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
Ven is short for Venerable, an archdeacon's title

explanation.surface: A clergyman regularly visits a cathedral city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like an alternate-letter signal, but it is the definition; Ely is the crossword's favourite cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: Evenly means at equal, steady intervals or in a uniform way, which is what regularly means.
